cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: The Roman family (familia) included everyone under the paterfamilias's authority — wife, children, slaves and dependants

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Patria potestas gave the father legal power over his children for life, even after they were adults

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Roman women could not vote or hold political office but managed households and could own and inherit property

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Marriage was typically arranged for political or economic reasons — the minimum age was 12 for girls

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Two types of marriage: cum manu (wife passed into husband's control) and sine manu (wife remained in father's control)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Divorce was relatively accessible — either party could initiate it, and dowry was usually returned

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Roman children were valued but infant mortality was high — children received a bulla (protective amulet) at birth

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Boys received formal education; girls were usually educated at home in domestic skills and literacy

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Upper-class women like Livia (wife of Augustus) and Cornelia (mother of the Gracchi) wielded significant influence

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: The Vestal Virgins were an exceptional group of women with unique religious and legal privileges

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Women participated in religious festivals and some public events, but were excluded from most political life

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Family & Women
cards.back: Roman epitaphs reveal affectionate marriages and grieving parents, challenging the image of purely transactional family life
